title: Seek the peace of the city (Jeremiah 29:4–7)
hook: a letter to the exiles: build houses, plant gardens, pray for the city you live in
carry: plant a garden there, and pray for the place

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah tried to keep quiet, and the word burned in him. Your line was silence turned out to be impossible. Did you say your sentence? Today, the prophet speaks by letter, to people far away. Day eight hundred four.

A letter goes out from Jerusalem, carried by messengers, to people who have been taken away to Babylon: elders, priests, prophets, craftsmen, ordinary families. They're living in a foreign city, the capital of the empire that conquered them. And some prophets among them are saying: don't unpack. This will be over soon. You'll be home before long. Jeremiah's letter says something else, and to people who wanted to hear go home, it is a hard letter.
screen: `A LETTER TO BABYLON.` → `DON'T UNPACK, SOME SAY.` → `JEREMIAH SAYS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the heart of it. "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them." Houses are for staying. Gardens take time to bear. Jeremiah is telling the exiles to stop waiting at the door. Marry, he goes on, have children, see your children married, increase there, and don't dwindle. Then the line that gives us today's title. "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." Read it twice. The city is Babylon. These are the people who conquered Jerusalem. And the exiles are told to seek its shalom, its peace, its welfare, and to pray for it. Not because Babylon deserves it, but because their lives are now tied to it: in its peace, your peace. Later in the same chapter the letter promises a return, but not soon. Until then, the instruction is to live fully where you are. A related teaching appears in the Mishnah. Pirkei Avot records Rabbi Chanina, the deputy high priest, saying: pray for the welfare of the government, for without fear of it, people would swallow one another alive. And in synagogue prayer books, there's a prayer for the country and its government, said on Shabbat. Jeremiah's letter asked something hard of people living somewhere they never chose: plant a garden there, and pray for the place.
screen: `BUILD HOUSES, PLANT GARDENS.` · then, large: `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.` · then: `IN ITS PEACE, YOUR PEACE.` · `PRAY FOR THE WELFARE OF THE GOVERNMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your town, or simply wish it well. Settle, and breathe. Bring your town or city to mind, the actual streets. The bus stop, the corner store, the school, the clinic, the park. Pick one place. Think of the people who work there, and the people who need it. Ask: what does this place's peace need right now? Fewer potholes, a kinder council meeting, a full food bank, a safe walk home. If you pray, you can hold Jeremiah's words for it: plant a garden there, and pray for the place. If you don't, hold the wish. Then find one small thing to do for it this week. The bell holds the time.
shalom, the peace Jeremiah told the exiles to seek for Babylon, the city that conquered them, and to pray for: for in its peace is yours. Today's word.
Your line: plant a garden there, and pray for the place. Today, do one small thing for the place you live: pick up, show up, or help out. Day eight hundred four.

howItsDone: In synagogue, a prayer for the welfare of the country and its government is said on Shabbat morning after the Torah reading, carrying forward Jeremiah's instruction to seek the peace of the city.

original.note: Hebrew: the peace (welfare) of the city, from Jeremiah 29:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to your neighbors.
what it means: exiles in the conquering city are told to build, plant, and pray for its peace, because their peace is bound up in it.
what a scholar hears: Pirkei Avot 3:2 carries the idea forward: pray for the welfare of the government, without which people would swallow one another.

sources.quoted: Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.

notes: Quoted from the KJV because I was not certain of the exact JPS 1917 wording.
The list of exiles (elders, priests, prophets, craftsmen, families) paraphrases 29:1–2; the prophets saying 'soon' paraphrases 29:8–9 and chapter 28.

The synagogue prayer for the government (e.g. Hanoten teshuah / prayer for the country) on Shabbat: the script and howItsDone describe it without quantifiers; customs vary, please check placement and wording.
The 'return, but not soon' refers to 29:10 without giving its number of years.

Editor: removed speculation about how the letter was received; Pirkei Avot 3:2 now presented as a related teaching (it does not cite Jeremiah), with Rabbi Chanina's title as deputy high priest; cut the stock phrase 'quietly radical'.

Audit: the teach's last line applied the instruction to 'anyone' (generalizing the command to the listener); now kept to the exiles. Keeper may like the echo of Isaiah 65:21 (day 796) in Jeremiah 29:5.
